description: Polish kingdom under the Jagiellonian dynasty (1385–1572) united with Lithuania and stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea; its defeat of the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (1410) established it as eastern Europe's dominant power, while the reign of Casimir IV and his successors made Poland-Lithuania a cultural and constitutional model for the region.

temporal.notes: Personal union with Lithuania via Krewo Union; later Lublin Union 1569

lifecycle_phases.description: Jogaila/Władysław II Jagiełło accepts baptism and marries Hedwig of Poland (1385–1386), founding the Jagiellonian dynasty. Combined Polish-Lithuanian forces defeat the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (1410), the largest medieval battle in European history. Casimir IV (1447–1492) defeats the Teutonic Order in the Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466), acquiring Royal Prussia and access to the Baltic. Poland becomes the largest country in Europe.

John I Albert (1492–1501) faces growing Ottoman and Tatar pressure in the southeast; a disastrous campaign against Moldova (1497) ends in Polish defeat in the Forest of Cosmin. The Jagiellonians rule Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia, and Hungary simultaneously in the early 16th century, the largest dynasty in Europe, before the Turkish conquest of Hungary (1526) and the union of Lublin (1569) reshape the political map.

rise_factors.description: The Jagiellonian dynasty's 186-year rule over Poland-Lithuania provided unprecedented political stability; the dynasty's expansion into Bohemia and Hungary through marriage created a central European empire that rivaled the Habsburgs

The combined Polish-Lithuanian army at Grunwald (1410) numbered 39,000 against the Teutonic Order's 27,000 in one of the largest battles of the Middle Ages; the combined cavalry traditions of Poland (heavy cavalry) and Lithuania (light cavalry and steppe tactics) created a versatile military force

The Polish-Lithuanian Union gave the Jagiellonian crown access to the vast eastern territories of Lithuania, stretching to the Black Sea, multiplying its military manpower and agricultural base; the Union of Horodło (1413) institutionalized the partnership that defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald

Poland exported grain through Gdańsk/Danzig to the Netherlands and England from the 15th century; this Baltic grain trade made Polish noble estates profitable and the export revenue funded royal courts and defensive infrastructure

The re-founded Jagiellonian University (1400) trained the royal administrators and diplomats who managed the complex Polish-Lithuanian double state; Copernicus studied there, the university's intellectual culture signaled Poland's full integration into European humanist networks

The Jagiellonian dynasty simultaneously ruled Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia, and Hungary in the late 15th century, creating the largest state complex in Europe and positioning Warsaw as a cultural and political center.

decline_factors.description: The Jagiellonian personal unions over Bohemia, Hungary, Poland, and Lithuania were too vast to administer coherently; the simultaneous Ottoman and Habsburg pressures from different directions exceeded the dynasty's ability to respond

The Polish nobility's liberum veto (formalized 1652 but rooted in this period) allowed any single noble to dissolve the Sejm; the structural disempowerment of the monarchy meant no army reforms, consistent taxation, or long-term military planning were achievable

The Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) to reclaim Prussian cities from the Teutonic Order exhausted Polish resources; though successful, the war demonstrated the difficulty of projecting power against well-fortified enemies and left the treasury depleted for decades

The liberum veto and increasingly powerful szlachta nobility progressively weakened royal authority, preventing the fiscal and military modernization needed to compete with centralized Prussia, Russia, and Austria.

sources.author: Davies, Norman
sources.title: God's Playground: A History of Poland, Vol. 1
